articles.title: Ground Zero first responder needed major surgery decades after 9/11 exposure: ‘I thought it was over’
articles.summary: Volunteer EMT Mordechai Shedrowitzky shares how Ground Zero dust exposure led to years of hospitalizations, steroids and a rare airway disease diagnosis.
articles.body: Those who were present at Ground Zero on Sept. 11, 2001, continue to experience the physical effects of their exposure. As Lower Manhattan was engulfed in dust and debris from the remnants of both towers, first responders and survivors were forced to breathe in toxic air. More than 400,000 people were exposed to toxic contaminants, physical-injury risks and stressful conditions in the days, weeks and months following the attacks, according to the World Trade Center Health Program. SCIENTISTS DISCOVER POSSIBLE LINK BETWEEN 9/11 AND ACCELERATED AGING As of March 2025, 8,215 people who had enrolled in the WTC Health Program had died, including 5,844 responders, as reported by the CDC. The figures include deaths from all causes; the program does not track whether a member’s death was related to 9/11 exposure. A responder’s long-term health battle In an interview with Fox News Digital, Mordechai Shedrowitzky, a volunteer EMT who responded on 9/11, shared how his exposure led to multiple hospitalizations and, ultimately, major surgery. Queens-born Shedrowitzky, 51, was living in Brooklyn at the time of the attacks. After helping cover his local area for much of the day, he headed into Lower Manhattan that evening to assist with the response. "My most vivid memory was actually entering Manhattan from Brooklyn," he said. "As we approached the tunnel, the first thing we noticed was there were no lights, there was no electricity in the area, it [was] pitch black." FOX NEWS' ERIC SHAWN REVEALS CANCER AND RESPIRATORY ILLNESS FROM 9/11 TOXIC DUST "When we entered the tunnel, there was a tremendous amount of swirling debris, at speeds that I just can't even imagine." Once Shedrowitzky and his team arrived at South Street Seaport, where his ambulance was staged with others, he described the debris as "overwhelming." "I remember the engine actually sputtering at times," he said. "I would imagine that it was taking in a tremendous amount of dust." "We were definitely not cognizant of what effect ... the air might have on us. And therefore, we did spend a significant amount of time outside of the ambulances, just commiserating with the people around us." Shedrowitzky said he "thought it was over" once he left the scene. But years later, he noticed small symptoms that were turning into a big problem. His pre-existing asthma — which typically flared during seasonal changes and caused coughing that required an inhaler — was worsening each year. AMERICA'S FIREFIGHTER SHORTAGE HITS CRISIS LEVEL AS EMERGENCY CALLS TRIPLE, PUTTING LIVES AT RISK "I started to require oral steroids," he said. "I would have wheezing; I would have coughing. It would last longer; it would be more serious ... I wouldn't be able to go to work, wouldn’t be able to take care of my kids. So, the effects were definitely increasing over time." Shedrowitzky added that his condition was "getting to the point where it was leading to frequent respiratory infections and hospitalizations." "It took a number of years, many years, for us to realize that what was going on with my health was probably related to 9/11." In 2019, Shedrowitzky described that his condition got "significantly worse," after experiencing a cough that wouldn’t resolve itself, even after the "highest doses" of steroids and antibiotics. NAVY VETERANS REUNITE AFTER 30 YEARS FOR 'GRUELING' CROSS-COUNTRY BIKE CHALLENGE HONORING 9/11 Shedrowitzky ultimately was put in touch with the World Trade Center Health Program – a federal program administered by the CDC – where his condition was classified as 9/11-related and was monitored. It was eventually confirmed that Shedrowitzky had tracheobronchomalacia, a condition in which the walls of the windpipe and major airways weaken and collapse during breathing. "[It] was probably secondary to both the asthma getting worse as well as steroid use over the years to try to treat those symptoms," he said. In 2024, Shedrowitzky underwent a procedure called a tracheobronchoplasty to structurally reinforce his trachea and main bronchi. RUDY GIULIANI REVEALS HE HAD 'SPIRITUAL EXPERIENCE' WHILE IN PNEUMONIA-RELATED COMA Two years after the procedure, he said he is feeling "much better," although he still experiences occasional infections. He hopes to return to work as a physical therapist soon. "Even a couple of months ago, I wouldn't have been able to speak for more than a very short time," Shedrowitzky said. "It took a number of years, many years, for us to realize that what was going on with my health was probably related to 9/11." As a father of six, Shedrowitzky – who is now also a grandfather of two – said his condition made it difficult for him to spend time with his children as they were growing up. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER "Things as simple as lifting my children, even speaking to them," he said. "The amount of time that I spent in the hospital and its effect on them was quite significant." "Now, they're older, but my ability to spend time, interact with them ... has been greatly improved." Treating 9/11-related illnesses Dr. Denise Harrison, medical director of the NYU Grossman School of Medicine WTC Health Program Clinical Center of Excellence, has been involved in post-9/11 healthcare since 2002. The program has since grown to provide screening, monitoring and treatment for people experiencing health effects related to their 9/11 exposure. The doctor noted that the dust on 9/11 was "highly alkaline," which can be "very irritating" to the airways. "Usually, the larger size dust gets deposited in the upper airways and the smaller size dust gets deposited in the lower airways," she told Fox News Digital. "Because of the overwhelming nature of the disaster, a significant number of large particles got deposited into the lower airways as well. So, this is not just the airways, but also the digestive tract, in the esophagus." Harrison said patients often report sinus problems, asthma and COPD. These conditions can occur alongside other "aerodigestive" issues, including gastroesophageal reflux disease, which may complicate diagnosis and treatment. CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES Other 9/11-related conditions may also be interlinked. "We have patients with asthma and PTSD who might perceive their asthma symptoms differently than the patients without PTSD, so that requires a combination of providers," the doctor said. Shedrowitzky urged other first responders who are experiencing health issues to not wait to get help and to confirm that what they’re experiencing may be linked to 9/11. "Continue to be monitored so that potential issues can be picked up early," he advised. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ "If we can look back and see the quality of life that it's robbing you of, it might push you to contact the World Trade Center Health Program, get the help that you need." As of March 31, 2025, the WTC Health Program had more than 130,000 currently enrolled members. The program, which is authorized through 2090, operates branches across multiple health systems, including NYU Langone Health, Mount Sinai, Northwell, Stony Brook and Rutgers. Harrison reiterated that the health effects of 9/11 exposure remain "persistent," and can be exacerbated by the environment and other illnesses. Experts predict that the fallout will continue for decades to come. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "Symptoms are still ongoing and research is still ongoing," she said, urging the public and responders to "have patience." "While it might not directly benefit them or may provide some benefits now, it could be more beneficial in the future and help the overall response to disasters."

articles.title: Going to airport, central Delhi or south Delhi? BRICS traffic restrictions you need to know
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Delhi will not be shut down during the BRICS Summit, but for commuters, the bigger worry may be the uncertainty on the roads: a route that .
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Delhi will not be shut down during the BRICS Summit, but for commuters, the bigger worry may be the uncertainty on the roads: a route that is open one minute could be stopped or diverted the next when a VVIP convoy approaches.The Delhi Traffic Police on Thursday clarified that normal traffic will continue wherever security arrangements permit, even as restrictions are imposed in notified controlled areas and on routes used by foreign delegations and dignitaries.But there is no fixed duration for traffic stoppages during VVIP movements, the traffic police said.Vehicles may be held temporarily or diverted depending on security requirements and the ground situation, before being released in phases, news agency PTI reported.For Delhi-NCR commuters, that could mean that simply checking whether a road is officially closed may not be enough.A regular route could remain open for most of the day but face sudden restrictions when a convoy moves through it.The real problem: unpredictable travel timeThe traffic plan announced ahead of the September 11-13 BRICS Summit at Bharat Mandapam covers more than 35 roads and 22 diversion points, with nearly 4,800 traffic personnel deployed for the arrangements.The restrictions are expected to remain in force from September 10 to around September 14.While Wednesday’s motorcade rehearsal gave commuters a preview of the congestion that can result from such arrangements, Thursday’s advisory makes clear that the disruption during the summit could vary depending on the movement of individual delegations.A visiting leader could have several high-security movements in a single day, from the airport to the hotel, the summit venue and then to bilateral meetings or other official engagements.Officials estimate that these could add up to 70-80 or more high-security movements across the city in a single day, PTI reported.Each movement requires traffic regulation and route coordination, meaning the impact could spread well beyond the immediate VVIP corridor.Noida, Dwarka, airport commuters could feel the ripple effectCommuters travelling between Noida and central Delhi, east Delhi and central areas, as well as those travelling from Dwarka and west Delhi towards Dhaula Kuan, the airport and south Delhi, are among those likely to be affected.As highlighted in the traffic plan, restrictions around central Delhi can push vehicles onto connecting roads, creating congestion even on stretches that are not themselves under a complete restriction.The movement of the Egyptian delegation between its hotel in Saket and central Delhi could add to pressure on south Delhi roads during peak hours.Traffic police had earlier suggested shifting the delegation’s accommodation closer to central Delhi to minimise the impact on traffic.A short stoppage can mean a much longer commuteThe issue for commuters is not necessarily that an entire road will remain closed.Traffic may instead be stopped briefly for a convoy and then released in phases. During that period, vehicles can accumulate behind the restriction, while diverted traffic adds pressure to alternative routes.This could make journey times difficult to predict, particularly for people travelling during peak office hours or those who have fixed reporting times, PTI reported.For daily commuters, students and people travelling to transport hubs, hospitals or examination centres, even a short VVIP stoppage could therefore have a knock-on effect on the rest of their journey.Candidates appearing for UPSC, NDA, CDS and other examinations have been advised to check their centres and routes beforehand, carry their admit cards and identification and leave sufficiently early.People travelling to hospitals for planned appointments have also been advised to allow additional time and check their routes in advance.In a genuine medical emergency, commuters have been asked to immediately inform nearby traffic personnel.Delhi Metro to remain operationalThe Delhi Metro will continue to operate during the summit, although temporary restrictions could be imposed at some stations or entry and exit gates if required for security reasons.DTC and city buses will also operate, but routes passing through affected areas could be diverted, curtailed or regulated.Inter-state buses may also face temporary changes in routes, entry points or termination points, PTI reported.Autos, taxis and app-based cabs will continue to operate, but their movement into controlled areas and pick-up and drop-off arrangements could be affected.Delivery services may similarly face restrictions in controlled areas, while movement of essential supplies such as milk and medicines will be facilitated under the applicable arrangements.Map apps to reflect diversions in real timeTraffic police have coordinated with online map service providers so that restrictions, diversions and alternate routes can be incorporated into navigation platforms in real time.Cab aggregators have also been advised against keeping pick-up and drop-off points inside restricted or controlled areas during VVIP movements.Heavy vehicles and trucks could face special restrictions on entry timings and routes and have been advised to check notified routes before travelling.Residents in controlled areas can move, with IDResidents living in notified controlled areas will not be completely barred from movement.They will be allowed to move subject to security arrangements and have been advised to carry valid identification and address proof and follow directions from police personnel.Parking on restricted and security-sensitive roads will not be permitted, with motorists advised to use designated parking facilities.‘Delhi bandh’ messages are fake, police warnThe traffic police has also cautioned commuters against forwarding unverified social media messages claiming that Delhi will observe a “bandh” or that there will be blanket road closures.The police has asked people to rely only on official traffic updates.For commuters, therefore, the challenge over the next few days may not be navigating a city-wide shutdown, but navigating a city where traffic conditions can change with every VVIP movement.With the summit bringing multiple delegations and potentially dozens of high-security movements each day, the question for a commuter may be less “Is my route closed?” and more “Will my route remain open by the time I reach it?”(With agency inputs)You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Delhi | Silver Rate in Delhi | Bank Holidays in Delhi | Public Holidays articles.title: Alcohol tied to surprising cancer death pattern in adults under 55, researchers find
articles.summary: Alcohol-attributable cancer deaths in the United States more than doubled from 1990 to 2023, with colorectal cancer surpassing liver cancer in younger men.
articles.body: Annual U.S. cancer deaths tied to alcohol consumption more than doubled over a three-decade period, according to a recent study led by researchers at the Sylvester Comprehensive Cancer Center at the University of Miami Miller School of Medicine. The findings, published in The Lancet Regional Health — Americas and presented at the American Society of Clinical Oncology Annual Meeting in Chicago, revealed that alcohol-attributable cancer deaths jumped from 11,361 in 1990 to 23,126 in 2023.
